title: Slicing Thick Tissue With Light
endLine: A pinhole rejects blur to slice thick tissue in three dimensions.

scenes.tts: Is that glowing speck inside the cell, or just sitting behind it? Under an ordinary microscope, thick glowing tissue turns hazy. Light from layers above and below floods the lens at once, collapsing depth into one flat blur.
scenes.caption: Is that glowing speck inside the cell, or just sitting behind it? Under an ordinary microscope, thick glowing tissue turns hazy. Light from layers above and below floods the lens at once, collapsing depth into one flat blur.
scenes.visual: A thick block of tissue fills the frame (schematic): a green branched cell surrounded by red and blue glowing specks. As an ordinary microscope lens focuses on the cell, haze from speckles above and below swells across the view, collapsing depth into one flat blurry overlay around the green cell and a red speck.
scenes.narration: Is that glowing speck inside the cell, or just sitting behind it? Under an ordinary microscope, thick glowing tissue turns hazy. Light from layers above and below floods the lens at once, collapsing depth into one flat blur.

scenes.visual: The glowing tissue block dims slightly in place as the title 'Slicing Thick Tissue With Light' appears across the centre in high-contrast type, then fades out while the tissue block remains.

scenes.tts: A confocal microscope clears that blur with a pinhole. Fluorescent dyes or antibodies make chosen structures glow as a focused laser scans one depth. Light from the focal spot comes back to a point, right at the pinhole. Light from other depths is spread wide there, so most hits the barrier around it.
scenes.caption: A confocal microscope clears that blur with a pinhole. Fluorescent dyes or antibodies make chosen structures glow as a focused laser scans one depth. Light from the focal spot comes back to a point, right at the pinhole. Light from other depths is spread wide there, so most hits the barrier around it.
scenes.visual: Above the same tissue block, the optical path builds in place (schematic): a laser beam narrows to a bright focal spot sweeping across one horizontal plane inside the tissue, making dyed structures glow. Bright rays from the focal spot converge straight through a small pinhole into a detector at top, while hazy rays from layers above and below spread wide and stop against the opaque barrier around the pinhole.
scenes.narration: A confocal microscope clears that blur with a pinhole. Fluorescent dyes or antibodies make chosen structures glow as a focused laser scans one depth. Light from the focal spot comes back to a point, right at the pinhole. Light from other depths is spread wide there, so most hits the barrier around it.

scenes.tts: Rejecting out-of-focus light with a pinhole yields a sharp optical section. It slices thick tissue with light instead of a blade. Step the focus deeper through intact tissue to collect a stack of clean slices. Software rebuilds that stack in three dimensions, showing where every labelled structure sits.
scenes.caption: Rejecting out-of-focus light with a pinhole yields a sharp optical section. It slices thick tissue with light instead of a blade. Step the focus deeper through intact tissue to collect a stack of clean slices. Software rebuilds that stack in three dimensions, showing where every labelled structure sits.
scenes.visual: In the same scene (schematic), the laser plane clears one crisp glowing slice and slides it into a vertical stack on the right. The focal plane steps downward through the intact tissue block, peeling off sharp slice after slice without cutting the block. The stack then fuses and gently rotates into a clean 3D reconstruction of the green branched cell and surrounding red and blue specks.

Step the focus deeper through intact tissue to collect a stack of clean slices. Software rebuilds that stack in three dimensions, showing where every labelled structure sits.

scenes.tts: Test that on our green cell. A red speck sits just above the cell, touching its outside. In a flat image, red overlaps green. When you step through a confocal stack, how can you tell the speck is outside?
scenes.caption: Test that on our green cell. A red speck sits just above the cell, touching its outside. In a flat image, red overlaps green. When you step through a confocal stack, how can you tell the speck is outside?
scenes.visual: Zoom into the same green cell inside the tissue block (schematic), with one bright red speck perched just above its upper surface. A quick top-down projection flashes the red speck sitting squarely on top of the green cell, then returns to the stacked slices with a focus plane ready to sweep and the question 'How does the stack show the speck is outside?' on screen.
scenes.narration: Test that on our green cell. A red speck sits just above the cell, touching its outside. In a flat image, red overlaps green. When you step through a confocal stack, how can you tell the speck is outside?

scenes.visual: The question remains on screen beside the green cell and the red speck perched above it, with gentle ambient shimmer in the glowing tissue and the focal-plane indicator hovering patiently (schematic).

scenes.tts: The speck peaks in a higher slice, outside the rebuilt cell, so software removes it. Raw volume misleads too: large cells hold more from size alone, so researchers divide internal label volume by cell volume. Independent checks show uptake. Label overlaps stained digestive compartments, which are acidic, so a dye that glows only in acid lights up.

scenes.visual: The focal plane sweeps upward through the stack (schematic): the red speck lights up in a slice above the green cell and vanishes as a 3D mask keeps only label inside the cell's volume. Next, a small and a large green cell appear side by side, each holding more label in proportion to its size, while the formula 'label volume inside ÷ cell volume' writes itself on screen as it is spoken (schematic, no numbers). Inside the cell, retained specks overlap a stained digestive compartment, which then brightens with an acid-activated glow.

scenes.tts: Two limits remain. Fixed tissue, chemically preserved, captures one frozen moment, and seeing a structure does not prove how it works. Counting stained branches can mislead too: one nerve cell branches widely, so counting endings does not count neurons.
scenes.caption: Two limits remain. Fixed tissue, chemically preserved, captures one frozen moment, and seeing a structure does not prove how it works. Counting stained branches can mislead too: one nerve cell branches widely, so counting endings does not count neurons.
scenes.visual: The glowing tissue block freezes into a still frame with a 'Fixed snapshot' tag as arrows asking how fluid or cargo moves fade into question marks (schematic). The tissue then shifts into a whole-mount skin sheet where a single glowing axon splits to wrap several hair follicles, highlighting that multiple stained endings trace back to one neuron (schematic).
scenes.narration: Two limits remain. Fixed tissue, chemically preserved, captures one frozen moment, and seeing a structure does not prove how it works. Counting stained branches can mislead too: one nerve cell branches widely, so counting endings does not count neurons.

scenes.tts: Those guards let confocal imaging open thick tissue. In 2004, Polsky, Mel and Schiller imaged thin dendrites, a neuron's input branches, in rat neocortex slices. They stimulated two sites, alone, then together. On one branch, nearby sites combined in an S-shape: slow, then steep, then level. Distant inputs simply added, supporting thin branches as separate subunits.

Distant inputs simply added, supporting thin branches as separate subunits.
scenes.visual: Inside the same optical-slice frame, a glowing pyramidal neuron appears in a rat neocortex slice (schematic, labelled 'Polsky, Mel & Schiller 2004'). The confocal focus locks onto one thin dendritic branch; two stimulation sites flash alone, then together. A graph builds beside it (schematic): bottom axis 'sum of separate responses', side axis 'response to both together', with a dashed 45-degree line. Nearby sites on one branch trace an S-shaped curve that rises slowly, then steeply, then levels off; moving the sites far apart puts the points on the dashed line.
scenes.narration: Those guards let confocal imaging open thick tissue. In 2004, Polsky, Mel and Schiller imaged thin dendrites, a neuron's input branches, in rat neocortex slices. Distant inputs simply added, supporting thin branches as separate subunits.

scenes.tts: In 2007, Baluk and colleagues imaged intact sheets of mouse trachea to see how fluid enters lymph vessels. In the first, blind-ended vessels, cells were joined by short buttons, about three point two micrometres long. Loose flaps lay between them. Larger collecting vessels had continuous, zipper-like junctions. From that structure alone, they proposed fluid enters between buttons.
scenes.caption: In 2007, Baluk and colleagues imaged intact sheets of mouse trachea to see how fluid enters lymph vessels. In the first, blind-ended vessels, cells were joined by short buttons, about 3.2 micrometres long. Loose flaps lay between them. Larger collecting vessels had continuous, zipper-like junctions. From that structure alone, they proposed fluid enters between buttons.
scenes.visual: The tissue block transforms into an intact whole mount of mouse trachea lit by the confocal scan (schematic, labelled 'Baluk et al. 2007'). In an initial lymphatic vessel, bright discontinuous button junctions appear along overlapping cell flaps (marked 'about 3.2 µm'), while a connected collecting vessel displays a continuous zipper-like seam. Dashed tentative arrows show proposed fluid entry between buttons, tagged 'inferred from structure'.

scenes.tts: In 2012, Schafer and colleagues dyed each eye's nerve endings a different colour in young mice. They rebuilt green microglia, brain immune cells, in the visual thalamus. Pieces of those endings sat inside digestive compartments, relatively more from a silenced eye. By rejecting blur, one pinhole turns crowded tissue into measurable space.
scenes.caption: In 2012, Schafer and colleagues dyed each eye's nerve endings a different colour in young mice. They rebuilt green microglia, brain immune cells, in the visual thalamus. scenes.visual: Return to our opening tissue world of the mouse visual thalamus (schematic, labelled 'Schafer et al. 2012'): the green microglial cell rebuilds in 3D as outer specks strip away, leaving red and blue retinal specks inside digestive compartments, with relatively more specks from the silenced eye's colour. The camera pulls back cleanly to the pinhole beam slicing the crowded tissue into sharp glowing planes.

scenes.visual: The optical slices fade smoothly into the dark background as the end-card sentence appears centred in clean high-contrast type: 'A pinhole rejects blur to slice thick tissue in three dimensions.'
